title: Cardinality, countability, and algebraic numbers
terms: cardinality; equinumerous sets; bijection; finite set; infinite set; countably infinite; count- able set; aleph-null; algebraic number; countable union.

exposition.text:
Two sets have the same cardinality when a bijection exists between them. A set is countably in-
finite if it is in bijection with N, and countable if finite or countably infinite. Integers, rationals,
finite tuples of integers, and algebraic numbers are countable. An algebraic number is a root of
a nonzero polynomial with integer coefficients.
A finite product and a countable union of countable sets are countable, under the usual set-
theoretic framework. For algebraic numbers, count polynomials by their finite coefficient lists
and use that each nonzero polynomial has finitely many roots. Infinite countable products are
different: all binary sequences already form an uncountable set. A countably infinite set can be
bijective with a proper subset, unlike a finite set.
The symbol ℵ (aleph-null) denotes |N|. Cardinal comparisons can be proved by injections:
0
|A| ≤ |B| means that an injection A → B exists. For example, selecting distinct rationals from
disjoint nonempty real intervals shows that such a family is at most countable, even though
each interval is uncountable.

question.text:
Which set is uncountable?
(A) All finite subsets of Z
(B) All polynomials with rational coefficients
(C) All real algebraic numbers
(D) All functions N → {0, 1}
(E) All ordered pairs of rational numbers

solution.text:
Finite subsets and finite coefficient lists form countable unions of finite products of count-
able sets. Algebraic numbers and rational pairs are countable. Binary sequences are
uncountable by the diagonal argument, since any purported listing misses the sequence
obtained by flipping its diagonal digits.

question.text:
How many real numbers can be roots of nonzero polynomials whose coefficients all belong to
{0, 1}?
(A) None
(B) Finitely many but nonzero
(C) Countably infinitely many
(D) Continuum many
(E) More than continuum many

solution.text:
There are countably many such finite coefficient strings, and each polynomial has finitely
many roots, so the set is countable. It is infinite: for each integer m ≥ 1, the polynomial
2m+1
1 + x + x has a root in (−1, 0) by the intermediate value theorem. Roots associated to
different m are distinct, since a shared root would give equal distinct powers of a number
with absolute value strictly between zero and one.

question.text:
A family of pairwise disjoint, nonempty open intervals in R is given. Which conclusion must
hold?
(A) The family is finite.
(B) The family is at most countable.
(C) Every interval has rational endpoints.
(D) The union is countable.
(E) All intervals have the same length.

solution.text:
Fix an enumeration of Q. From each interval select the first rational in that enumeration
that lies inside it. Density guarantees such a rational, and disjointness makes the selected
rationals distinct. This injects the family into Q. A single interval is already uncountable,
so the union need not be countable.

question.text:
If A is countably infinite and B ⊆ A, which must hold?
(A) B is countably infinite
(B) B is finite
(C) P(B) is countable
(D) A \ B is finite
(E) B is finite or countably infinite

solution.text:
A subset of an enumerated set can be listed by retaining its members in that enumer-
ation. It may be finite, but cannot be uncountable; its power set may nevertheless be
uncountable.
